disclaimer: Only milestones confirmed word for word in the sources; methodological divergences (the 2007 GDP revision, Treasury vs. FGV/Ibre series) are documented in the methodology.
eras[0].note: A system leaning on foreign trade and cascading taxes. The burden climbs slowly, from 13.8% to ~19% of GDP.
eras[1].note: Constitutional Amendment 18/1965 and the tax code create the ICM and IPI. In five years the burden jumps from 19% to 26% of GDP — the largest rise in so short a time in Brazilian history.
eras[2].note: The burden hovers at 24–26% and falls to 22.4% in 1988, eroded by crisis and high inflation. The Constitution decentralises revenue.
eras[3].note: To offset decentralisation, the union multiplies the contributions it shares with nobody: CSLL, Cofins, then IPMF/CPMF.
eras[4].note: The currency stabilised — and the burden took off: ~10 points of GDP more in the two decades after the Real, reaching 33.64% in 2007.
eras[5].note: Steady between 31% and 34%: relief only in the pandemic (31.64% in 2020) and a record in 2024. The Scandinavian level arrived; the Scandinavian services did not.
empire.finding: There is no reliable % of GDP for the 19th century — national accounts did not exist. What the historiography does document: the empire of Dom Pedro II lived on the import duty, which accounted for half or more of central government revenue (above 60% in some years). The average customs tariff went from ~17% in the 1830s to almost 50% by the late 1880s. Taxing everything that comes in: the habit is older than the republic.
empire.ruler: The ruler of the 19th century is not the ruler of the 21st, and pretending otherwise would be the very flaw this site holds others to. There were no national accounts under the Empire: "tax burden as a share of GDP" does not exist for the period, because GDP was not measured. What does exist, and it is in the table below, is WHERE every unit of central-government revenue came from.
empire.tariff: The import tariff rose throughout the Empire. The ratio between import duties collected and the value of imports stayed around 17% in the 1830s, climbed fast in the 1840s with the 1844 Alves Branco tariff, held between 25% and 30% until the late 1860s, then rose to 35–40% and reached almost 50% by the end of the 1880s.
empire.denominatorCaveat: A caveat the study itself demands, and it changes how one of the bars reads: the paper says the import tax was "always above 50%" of the central government’s ORDINARY revenue after 1833, while the table measures the share of TOTAL revenue. Those are different denominators, which is why 1830-31 appears here at 22.1%. We publish the table as it is, with the study’s own sentence beside it — splicing the two into a single figure would be swapping rulers mid-series.
tiradentes.headline: Tiradentes died over a lighter tax than the one we accept today.
tiradentes.finding: The Portuguese Crown charged the quinto: about 20% of all gold mined in Minas Gerais. When the annual quota of 100 arrobas fell short, the derrama followed — the shortfall collected by force, at gunpoint. It was the threat of the 1789 derrama that set off the Inconfidência Mineira; Tiradentes was hanged and quartered on 21 April 1792. Today the Brazilian state keeps 32.40% of everything the country produces and around 41% of the average worker's income — and the derrama is automatic: deducted from the payslip and embedded in the shelf price, no troops required.
tiradentes.caveat: Different bases, an honest comparison: the quinto fell on gold mined; today's burden falls on all income and consumption. The order of magnitude still speaks for itself.
burdenMilestones[8].divergence.note: The Treasury calculates 29.15% for 2020, on the national-accounts methodology. The gap between the two rulers is systematic: in every one of the fifteen years where both exist, the Treasury sits 1.65 to 2.47 points below FGV/Ibre.
burdenMilestones[9].divergence.note: FGV/Ibre calculates 34.24% for 2024, on a different methodology. And the Treasury itself revised the year to 32.22% in the following bulletin — its series is restated with every edition.
burdenSeries.metric: Gross tax burden as % of GDP, year by year, on the two rulers that measure it today
burdenSeries.scope: The two columns measure the SAME thing and are not the same number: in every one of the fifteen years where both exist, the Treasury sits 1.65 to 2.47 points below FGV/Ibre. The difference is methodological, not an error, and it disappears if anyone splices the two into a single line. Before 1990 neither exists: what reaches back to 1947 are the Varsano/Ipea milestones in `burdenMilestones`, a third ruler that does not splice with these.
burdenRulers.varsano: The Varsano/Ipea series (working paper 583), reconstructed for 1947-1994. It is the only source that reaches the period, and it does not compare point by point with the two that follow.
burdenRulers.fgvIbre: FGV/Ibre's Fiscal Policy Observatory, from 1990 onwards. It calculates systematically ABOVE the Treasury — in 2024, 34.24% against 32.22%.
burdenRulers.tesouro: The National Treasury, Gross Tax Burden of General Government, from 2010 onwards. It is the official national-accounts ruler, and the one the government announces.
tenthPenny.headline: Ten per cent was enough — and the tax was never even collected.
tenthPenny.finding: In March 1569 the Duke of Alba announced to the Low Countries a general, permanent 10 per cent sales tax, the Tenth Penny, to give the central government financial independence. Britannica records the effect: the proposal "had united Roman Catholics and Calvinists against Spain and breathed life into the rebellion". The tax was only due to take effect in 1571, and was never collected. The proposal alone was enough.
tenthPenny.caveat: A comparison of rates, not of eras: the 10 per cent fell on every sale, and Brazil's burden today adds up taxes on different bases. What is being compared here is the THRESHOLD — how much a society finds acceptable before it asks why. In 1569, ten per cent united against the same tax people who united over nothing else. A R$ 100 purchase from a foreign site outside the Remessa Conforme programme pays R$ 92.77, by the Revenue Service's own arithmetic.
tenthPenny.closing: The difference between the two eras is not the rate. It is how much counts as normal.
tenthPenny.source: Britannica — entry "Council of Troubles"; Federal Revenue Service — New Rules, Example 2.1
